[PATH:empirical] Multi-regional input-output (MRIO) databases such as EXIOBASE 3 or GTAP, combined with material flow accounts (e.g., Eurostat, UNEP IRP), analyzing trends in raw material consumption (RMC) vs. material footprint over 1990–2019 for high-income countries. — This source directly tests whether absolute decoupling is artifact of trade displacement by comparing domestic material use (apparent decoupling) with total material footprint including imports, thus revealing relocation of resource extraction and processing.

[PATH:empirical] Panel data econometric studies linking changes in high-income countries' material footprint to shifts in middle- and low-income countries' resource extraction intensity and export volumes, using instruments for trade openness and environmental regulation. — Such analysis can confirm causality between decoupling in high-income nations and increased material use elsewhere, addressing the 'relocation versus genuine reduction' dispute by controlling for income and technology effects.

[PATH:literature] Life-cycle assessment (LCA) meta-literature on specific material-intensive products (e.g., electronics, steel, cement) that tracks global supply chains and environmental burdens across income groups from 1990–2019. — This provides qualitative and quantitative evidence on how consumption patterns in high-income countries externalize ecological costs, corroborating or refuting the claim that global ecological limits are merely shifted rather than reduced.

scope.domain: empirical economics / material flow analysis / global trade

qualifier.geographic: high-income countries (World Bank classification), with embodied resource flows from middle- and low-income countries

[PATH:empirical] Multi-regional input-output (MRIO) database analysis (e.g., EXIOBASE, GTAP) tracking material footprints and embodied resource flows between high-income and lower-income countries from 1990–2019 — Directly tests whether apparent absolute decoupling in high-income countries is offset by increased resource use in lower-income countries via offshoring, measuring net global material consumption.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of published material flow accounts (e.g., Wiedmann et al., 2015; Hickel & Kallis, 2020) focusing on long-term trends in domestic material consumption vs. material footprint — Synthesizes existing empirical evidence to assess whether observed decoupling in high-income countries is genuine or an artifact of trade displacement, and whether global resource use is declining or rising.

[PATH:empirical] Empirical panel regression of GDP growth, material footprint, and trade openness for OECD vs. non-OECD countries (1990–2019) — Quantifies the statistical relationship between high-income decoupling, offshoring intensity, and global resource use trends, providing causal evidence to confirm or refute the masking hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Historical analysis of GDP-emissions decoupling rates across developed economies (e.g., EU, US, Japan) from 1990-2020, focusing on periods of >2% GDP growth and net negative emissions sectors — Provides real-world data on whether absolute decoupling has been achieved under sustained high growth, directly testing the feasibility of the hypothesis without DACCS.

[PATH:theoretical] Integrated assessment model (IAM) scenario comparison: SSP1-1.9 vs SSP2-1.9 with and without large-scale DACCS deployment, as reported in the IPCC AR6 WGIII database — Enables quantitative comparison of emission pathways under continued >2% GDP growth, isolating the contribution of DACCS versus demand-side reductions to meeting the 1.5°C target.

[PATH:literature] Review of carbon capture and storage (CCS) cost and scalability literature, including lifecycle analysis of DACCS permanence and leakage rates (e.g., National Academies report on negative emissions technologies) — Evaluates whether large-scale DACCS with geological storage is technically and economically viable at the required scale, a necessary condition for the hypothesis to hold.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of peer-reviewed literature on energy intensity improvements and renewable penetration projections (e.g., from IPCC AR6 WGIII, IEA WEO, and review papers by Grubler et al. 2018). — Synthesizes existing expert consensus on maximum achievable efficiency gains and renewable deployment rates, identifying whether historical limits and modeled ceilings support the claim of full decoupling without complementary measures.
